source_refs.note: Exercise 10.1, Question 6: book page 278 (Q1-Q24). The book prints no answers for Exercise 10.1.

blocks.explanation:
Both terms are squares of sine and cosine of the same angle.
Dividing by \(\cos^{2}x\) gives one ratio: \(\tan^{2}x = 3\).
Plan: first make sure \(\cos x = 0\) is not a solution, then solve \(\tan x = \pm\sqrt{3}\) with period \(\pi\).
steps:
Given: \(\sin^{2}x - 3\cos^{2}x = 0\).
To find: principal solutions and general solution.
Method: divide by \(\cos^{2}x\) to get an equation in \(\tan x\) only.

Can \(\cos x = 0\)?
If \(\cos x = 0\), then \(\sin^{2}x = 1\) and the left side is \(1 - 0 = 1 \ne 0\).
Why: we may divide by \(\cos^{2}x\) only if no solution is lost; this shows none is.

Divide by \(\cos^{2}x\)
\[\dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x} - 3 = 0\]
\[\tan^{2}x = 3\]
\[\tan x = \pm\sqrt{3}\]
Why: \(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x\); a square root has two signs.

When \(\tan x = \sqrt{3}\) (quadrants I, III)
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\]
\[x = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\]
Why: tangent is positive in quadrants I and III.

When \(\tan x = -\sqrt{3}\) (quadrants II, IV)
\[x = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\]
\[x = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\]
Why: tangent is negative in quadrants II and IV.

General solution
The period of \(\tan x\) is \(\pi\); \(\frac{4\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{3} + \pi\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3} + \pi\):
\[\left\{\dfrac{\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\}\]
\[\cup \left\{\dfrac{2\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\]
Why: tangent repeats after every \(\pi\).

Check
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}:\ \dfrac{3}{4} - 3\cdot\dfrac{1}{4} = 0\]
Why: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\). At the other three angles \(\sin^{2}x = \frac{3}{4}\) and \(\cos^{2}x = \frac{1}{4}\) as well.
blocks.final_answer: Principal solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{4\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{3}\). General solution: \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\}\) \(\cup\) \(\left\{\frac{2\pi}{3} + n\pi\right\}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 10.1. Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. As in the book's examples, we give the principal solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\) and the general solution as a union of sets.
